title: Management and prevention of bone stress injuries in long-distance runners
authors: Warden SJ, Davis IS, Fredericson M
journal: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
population: Long-distance runners with, or at risk of, bone stress injury; a clinical commentary (level of evidence 5) with no original data
findings: Bone stress injury (BSI) is the inability of bone to withstand repetitive loading, which results in structural fatigue and localised bone pain and tenderness. It lies on a continuum from stress reaction to stress fracture and, ultimately, a complete bone fracture.
Most BSIs heal following a period of modified loading and a progressive return to running, but they tend to recur, which the authors read as a need to address the underlying causes.

A BSI results from disruption of the balance between microdamage formation and its removal. Microdamage accumulation, and so the risk of a BSI, relates both to the load applied to a bone and to the ability of the bone to resist load.

The authors call the applied load the more amenable factor and name training-program design, lowering impact forces (for example a higher stride rate) and strengthening local muscles as ways to change it; they also point to malalignment and abnormal movement patterns.
limitations: Clinical commentary at level of evidence 5 (expert opinion): no new data, and the abstract states no search method. The abstract gives no time course of bone adaptation and no safe rate of increase in running. Abstract read; the full text is behind a paywall and was not read.
implications: Supplies the framework for bone stress injury (microdamage against its removal, load against the bone's ability to resist it); it frames why load changes matter, with no threshold.
States nothing the engine can turn into a number: no time course of adaptation, no weekly increase, no credit for earlier training.

verification.notes: Crossref 2026-10-25: title, JOSPT 44(10):749-765, 2014-10, three authors and DOI match. Europe PMC abstract (PMID 25103133) read; the level of evidence (therapy, level 5) is in it. Full text not read, so no claim beyond the abstract is made.
